title: Three days
hook: mourning is three days, and a widow's waiting period is longer (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the burial: quickly, facing the qiblah, into the earth. Your line: back to the earth. Did you find some ground to rest a hand on? Today, the people walking home from the grave. Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

Zaynab bint Abi Salamah tells this one, in Sahih al-Bukhari. News came to Umm Habibah, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that her father had died. She waited. Then, on the third day, she called for perfume, a yellowish scent, and rubbed some on her arms and face. And she explained herself, in paraphrase: I have no need of perfume. I'm doing this because I heard the Prophet say that a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day should not mourn anyone more than three days, except a husband. A daughter who has just lost her father, putting on perfume. On purpose. Today: why she did it.
screen: `NEWS OF HER FATHER.` → `ON THE THIRD DAY, PERFUME.` → `I HAVE NO NEED OF IT.`

segments.voice: The perfume was a signal, and the signal was: the outward mourning is finished. The hadith speaks to a believing woman: three days is the limit of this outward mourning for anyone but a husband. For those days, grief is given room, and adornment, like perfume, is set aside. And then, by the Prophet's word, that outward season closes. Umm Habibah wasn't saying she'd stopped missing her father. She said plainly she had no need of the perfume. She was honoring the limit. So the first thing here is permission: grief gets real time. Three days is not a moment. The second thing is a boundary: the formal mourning doesn't swallow a life whole. The same hadith names one exception, a widow, and the Qur'an gives that waiting its own measure. In surah al-Baqarah, women whose husbands have died are to wait, keeping to themselves, four months and ten days, and then, the verse says, there's no blame on them for what they decide for themselves in a fitting way. That period is called the 'iddah. Some readers see it as longer because more has ended: a household, a marriage, a whole shape of life. So there are two clocks. A short one for mourning a relative, and a longer one for the person whose life was most rearranged. Neither clock says the love has stopped. What they do is give grief a container. It has a beginning, a middle, and a door out. And the people around the grieving know when to come close, and when to let them rise.
screen: `THE PERFUME WAS A SIGNAL.` · `GRIEF GETS REAL TIME.` · `A LONGER WAITING FOR A WIDOW.` · `A CONTAINER WITH A DOOR OUT.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit with the grieving. You don't have to go anywhere for this. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has lost a person, recently or long ago. Picture sitting beside them. No advice. No fixing. Just being there, the way a visitor might in those first days. Notice whether saying nothing is hard, and how much the sitting itself can say. If someone comes to mind who is in their first days of grief, hold their name for a few breaths. If you pray, you can remember them and the one they lost. The bell holds the time.
Three days. The time of outward mourning for a relative in the hadith, with a longer waiting, the 'iddah, for a widow. Today's word.

Your line: three days of mourning. If someone you know is grieving, reach out today with a short message that asks nothing of them. Tomorrow, food for the bereaved. Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims observe a period of mourning for a relative, which a hadith in al-Bukhari limits to three days, while a widow keeps a longer waiting period, the 'iddah, described in Qur'an 2:234

original.note: Arabic: the waiting period, here a widow's, set in al-Baqarah.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims mourn for three days and that's it.
what it means: three days of outward mourning for a relative, a longer waiting for a widow, and neither one says the love has ended.
what a scholar hears: Umm Habibah's perfume in al-Bukhari, and al-Baqarah 2:234's four months and ten days.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1280–1281 (Umm Habibah's perfume; mourning three days except for a husband)
Qur'an 2:234 (widows wait four months and ten days)

notes: Editor: the teach now says the hadith addresses a believing woman's outward mourning (setting aside adornment such as perfume) instead of generalizing to community visits; cut unsourced 'people come, people sit'; the reason the widow's waiting is longer is now framed as a reading ('some readers'); howItsDone no longer claims visiting customs.
Bukhari 1280–1281 paraphrased; confirm numbers, that Zaynab bint Abi Salamah narrates, and the detail of the yellowish perfume on her arms/face.
The hadith addresses women's mourning; the teach generalizes 'three days' to formal mourning for a relative. Confirm this framing (some jurists apply condolence visits to three days generally).
